content.text: Programming Diagnostic
This diagnostic shows what you remembered today. Use the topic and skill indicators to choose what to practise next.
Variables
Trace stored values, use meaningful identifiers and write a simple assignment in your chosen language.

content.prompt: What does an assignment statement do?

options.label: Stores a value under a variable name

feedback.correct: Assignment stores a value under a variable name so the program can use or update it later.
feedback.incorrect: Assignment stores a value under a variable name so the program can use or update it later.

content.prompt: What value is output?

feedback.correct: The value starts at 5 and has 3 added twice, so the program outputs 11.
feedback.incorrect: The value starts at 5 and has 3 added twice, so the program outputs 11.

content.prompt: Create a variable called score and give it the whole-number value 10.

feedback.correct: The declaration creates score and assigns the integer value 10 using the selected language's normal syntax.
feedback.incorrect: The declaration creates score and assigns the integer value 10 using the selected language's normal syntax.

content.prompt: Match each value to the most suitable conceptual data type.

feedback.correct: Text stores characters, integers store whole numbers, decimals store fractional numbers and Booleans store true or false.
feedback.incorrect: Text stores characters, integers store whole numbers, decimals store fractional numbers and Booleans store true or false.

content.prompt: Complete the update so that lives becomes 2 before it is output.

feedback.correct: Subtracting 1 from the current value 3 updates lives to 2.
feedback.incorrect: Subtracting 1 from the current value 3 updates lives to 2.

content.text: Selection
Use Boolean conditions to predict, complete and debug branches in your chosen language.

content.prompt: Which condition is true when age is 18?

feedback.correct: The >= operator means greater than or equal to, so it includes the value 18.
feedback.incorrect: The >= operator means greater than or equal to, so it includes the value 18.

content.prompt: Which word is output?

feedback.correct: 72 is below 80 but at least 60, so the middle branch outputs Silver.
feedback.incorrect: 72 is below 80 but at least 60, so the middle branch outputs Silver.

content.prompt: Complete the condition so Adult is output when age is 18 or above.

feedback.correct: The >= operator includes 18 and every value above 18.
feedback.incorrect: The >= operator includes 18 and every value above 18.

content.prompt: Select the line containing the faulty comparison.

feedback.correct: The condition must compare age with 18. A single equals sign performs assignment rather than equality comparison.
feedback.incorrect: The condition must compare age with 18. A single equals sign performs assignment rather than equality comparison.

content.prompt: Complete the program with a branch that outputs Adult when age is 18 or above.

feedback.correct: A correct branch compares age with the inclusive boundary and outputs Adult inside that branch.
feedback.incorrect: A correct branch compares age with the inclusive boundary and outputs Adult inside that branch.

content.text: Iteration
Trace loops, complete boundaries and order a condition-controlled loop safely.

content.prompt: Why is iteration useful?

options.label: It repeats instructions under a defined condition
It always chooses between two branches

feedback.correct: A loop repeats instructions while a condition holds or for a controlled number of times.
feedback.incorrect: A loop repeats instructions while a condition holds or for a controlled number of times.

content.prompt: How many times is Tick output?

feedback.correct: The loop uses counter values 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, so Tick is output five times.
feedback.incorrect: The loop uses counter values 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, so Tick is output five times.

content.prompt: Complete the loop so it outputs the numbers 1 to 5.

feedback.correct: The loop starts at 1 and includes 5 without continuing to 6.
feedback.incorrect: The loop starts at 1 and includes 5 without continuing to 6.

content.prompt: Select the line that causes an out-of-range access.

feedback.correct: The loop creates one index beyond the final valid position in the three-item collection.
feedback.incorrect: The loop creates one index beyond the final valid position in the three-item collection.

content.prompt: Reorder the code so it outputs 1, 2 and 3, then stops.

feedback.correct: A working loop initialises the counter, checks the boundary, outputs the value and then updates the counter.
feedback.incorrect: A working loop initialises the counter, checks the boundary, outputs the value and then updates the counter.

content.text: Functions
Connect parameters and return values, then complete and write a small reusable function.

content.prompt: What is a main benefit of placing a repeated calculation in a function?

options.label: It can be named, reused and tested separately
It is guaranteed to run faster
It removes the need for inputs

feedback.correct: A named function decomposes a program into a reusable unit that can be understood and tested separately.
feedback.incorrect: A named function decomposes a program into a reusable unit that can be understood and tested separately.

content.prompt: Match each function term to its meaning.

items.text: A named input in a function definition
A value supplied when a function is called
A value sent back to the caller

feedback.correct: A parameter names an expected input, an argument is the supplied value, and a return value is sent back to the caller.
feedback.incorrect: A parameter names an expected input, an argument is the supplied value, and a return value is sent back to the caller.

rows.label: A named input in a function definition
A value supplied when a function is called
A value sent back to the caller

content.prompt: What value is output?

feedback.correct: The function receives 4 and 6, adds them and returns 10 to the caller.
feedback.incorrect: The function receives 4 and 6, adds them and returns 10 to the caller.

content.prompt: Complete the function so it returns the square of number.

feedback.correct: Returning number multiplied by itself gives the square to the caller.
feedback.incorrect: Returning number multiplied by itself gives the square to the caller.

content.prompt: Write a function called double_number/DoubleNumber that returns twice its supplied whole number.

feedback.correct: The function accepts one number and returns that number multiplied by 2.
feedback.incorrect: The function accepts one number and returns that number multiplied by 2.

content.text: Arrays/Lists
Read, update, create and safely iterate through an indexed collection.

content.prompt: When is an array/list more suitable than separate variables?

options.label: When storing related values such as weekly scores
When storing one fixed course title
Only when storing true or false
Only when a database is unavailable

feedback.correct: Arrays and lists keep related values together and allow the same processing across the collection.
feedback.incorrect: Arrays and lists keep related values together and allow the same processing across the collection.

content.prompt: Which colour is output?

feedback.correct: Zero-based indexing makes red index 0 and green index 1.
feedback.incorrect: Zero-based indexing makes red index 0 and green index 1.

content.prompt: Complete the index so the second score changes from 6 to 10.

feedback.correct: The second item in a zero-indexed collection is at index 1.
feedback.incorrect: The second item in a zero-indexed collection is at index 1.

content.prompt: Create a collection called students containing Aisha, Ben and Chloe in that order.

feedback.correct: The collection declaration stores the three text values in the requested order.
feedback.incorrect: The collection declaration stores the three text values in the requested order.

content.prompt: Select the loop line that accesses one position beyond the final item.

feedback.correct: A collection of length 3 has valid indexes 0, 1 and 2, so the loop boundary must exclude 3.
feedback.incorrect: A collection of length 3 has valid indexes 0, 1 and 2, so the loop boundary must exclude 3.

content.text: Debugging
Identify faulty lines and edit small programs to correct syntax and logic errors.

content.prompt: Select the line containing the faulty equality comparison.

feedback.correct: The faulty line assigns a value where the condition needs an equality comparison.
feedback.incorrect: The faulty line assigns a value where the condition needs an equality comparison.

content.prompt: Fix the boundary so the discount applies to totals of 50 or more.

feedback.correct: The inclusive >= comparison applies the discount at 50 and above.
feedback.incorrect: The inclusive >= comparison applies the discount at 50 and above.

content.prompt: Select the line that causes the collection boundary error.

feedback.correct: The loop must stop before the collection length because indexing starts at zero.
feedback.incorrect: The loop must stop before the collection length because indexing starts at zero.

content.prompt: Correct the inconsistent variable name in the final calculation.

feedback.correct: Variable names must match exactly, including underscores and capital letters.
feedback.incorrect: Variable names must match exactly, including underscores and capital letters.

content.prompt: Edit the function so it returns the calculated area to its caller.

feedback.correct: The function needs a return statement that sends the calculated area back to the caller.
feedback.incorrect: The function needs a return statement that sends the calculated area back to the caller.

content.text: Basic SQL
Complete and debug shared SQL statements without connecting to or changing a live database.

content.prompt: Match each relational database term to its meaning.

items.text: A structured collection about one subject
One complete row about an item
A value that uniquely identifies each row

feedback.correct: Tables contain records, records contain fields, and a primary key uniquely identifies each record.
feedback.incorrect: Tables contain records, records contain fields, and a primary key uniquely identifies each record.

rows.label: A structured collection about one subject
One complete row about an item
A value that uniquely identifies each row

content.prompt: Which first name is returned by this query?

feedback.correct: WHERE active = true keeps only C01, and SELECT first_name returns Amina.
feedback.incorrect: WHERE active = true keeps only C01, and SELECT first_name returns Amina.

content.prompt: Complete the query so it returns only Premium customers.

feedback.correct: A WHERE clause filters rows, and the text value Premium is written in quotes.
feedback.incorrect: A WHERE clause filters rows, and the text value Premium is written in quotes.

content.prompt: Reorder the fragments to form a valid INSERT statement.

feedback.correct: INSERT INTO names the table, the field list identifies the columns, and VALUES supplies the new row.
feedback.incorrect: INSERT INTO names the table, the field list identifies the columns, and VALUES supplies the new row.

content.prompt: Edit the statement so it updates only customer C02.

feedback.correct: WHERE customer_id = 'C02' limits the update to one known record; without it every row would change.
feedback.incorrect: WHERE customer_id = 'C02' limits the update to one known record; without it every row would change.

metadata.title: Requirements Classification
metadata.summary: Distinguish what a solution must do from the qualities and constraints it must meet.
metadata.detail: Classify realistic requirements, then decide whether requirements are testable.

content.text: Requirements Classification
Use the result to review how actions, qualities and measurable constraints are expressed in requirements.
Classify the requirements

Northbridge College wants an equipment-loan service for cameras, laptops and audio kits. A functional requirement describes what the solution must do. A non-functional requirement describes a quality, constraint or condition for how it operates.

content.prompt: Students can search available equipment by name, category or collection date.

feedback.correct: This describes actions the solution must perform: searching records using three criteria.
feedback.incorrect: This describes actions the solution must perform: searching records using three criteria.

content.prompt: Search results must appear within two seconds for at least 95% of searches during college opening hours.

feedback.correct: The response-time target is a measurable performance quality rather than a user action.
feedback.incorrect: The response-time target is a measurable performance quality rather than a user action.

content.prompt: A student can reserve one available item for a selected collection slot.

feedback.correct: Reserving an item and selecting a slot are behaviours the solution must provide.
feedback.incorrect: Reserving an item and selecting a slot are behaviours the solution must provide.

content.prompt: The service must support the current and previous major versions of Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge.

feedback.correct: Supported browsers are a compatibility constraint on how the service must operate.
feedback.incorrect: Supported browsers are a compatibility constraint on how the service must operate.

content.prompt: Technicians can mark an item as unavailable and record the reason.

feedback.correct: Updating an item's status and storing a reason are system functions.
feedback.incorrect: Updating an item's status and storing a reason are system functions.

content.prompt: The service must remain usable when the page is enlarged to 200% without loss of content or controls.

feedback.correct: This sets a measurable accessibility and usability quality for the interface.
feedback.incorrect: This sets a measurable accessibility and usability quality for the interface.

content.prompt: When a reservation is confirmed, the service stores the student ID, item ID, collection slot and reservation time.

feedback.correct: The requirement specifies data the solution must store when an event occurs.
feedback.incorrect: The requirement specifies data the solution must store when an event occurs.

content.prompt: Only authorised technicians can view the equipment maintenance notes.

feedback.correct: This is an access-control and security constraint on who may see sensitive operational information.
feedback.incorrect: This is an access-control and security constraint on who may see sensitive operational information.

content.prompt: A student can cancel a reservation until 30 minutes before its collection slot.

feedback.correct: Cancellation is a user action. The time rule constrains that function but the main requirement still describes behaviour.
feedback.incorrect: Cancellation is a user action. The time rule constrains that function but the main requirement still describes behaviour.

content.prompt: The service must be available from 07:00 to 20:00 on teaching days, excluding published maintenance periods.

feedback.correct: This sets a measurable availability condition rather than describing a transaction.
feedback.incorrect: This sets a measurable availability condition rather than describing a transaction.

content.prompt: The service shows a clear reason when a reservation cannot be completed.

feedback.correct: Displaying an explanatory result after a failed action is behaviour the solution must perform.
feedback.incorrect: Displaying an explanatory result after a failed action is behaviour the solution must perform.

content.prompt: Reservation data must be encrypted while travelling between the browser and the service.

feedback.correct: Encryption in transit is a security condition on how data is handled.
feedback.incorrect: Encryption in transit is a security condition on how data is handled.

content.prompt: Technicians can produce a list of overdue items grouped by equipment category.

feedback.correct: Generating and grouping an overdue-items list is an output the solution must provide.
feedback.incorrect: Generating and grouping an overdue-items list is an output the solution must provide.

content.prompt: A first-time student should be able to reserve an available item in no more than five minutes without staff help.

feedback.correct: This expresses a measurable usability target for completing the reservation process.
feedback.incorrect: This expresses a measurable usability target for completing the reservation process.

content.text: Requirement quality challenge
A useful requirement gives a tester enough information to decide whether the solution meets it. Decide whether each requirement is testable as written.

content.prompt: The equipment search should load quickly.

feedback.correct: Quickly has no shared measurement. A response-time threshold and a defined test condition would make it testable.
feedback.incorrect: Quickly has no shared measurement. A response-time threshold and a defined test condition would make it testable.

content.prompt: Search results must be displayed within two seconds when the catalogue contains up to 10,000 items.

feedback.correct: The two-second limit and catalogue size give a tester a measurable expected result and condition.
feedback.incorrect: The two-second limit and catalogue size give a tester a measurable expected result and condition.

content.prompt: The system should be easy for students to use.

feedback.correct: Easy is subjective without a defined user group, task and success measure.
feedback.incorrect: Easy is subjective without a defined user group, task and success measure.

content.prompt: At least 8 of 10 first-time student testers must complete a reservation within five minutes without staff help.

feedback.correct: The user group, task, time limit, sample size and success threshold can all be observed.
feedback.incorrect: The user group, task, time limit, sample size and success threshold can all be observed.

content.prompt: The service must work well in modern browsers.

feedback.correct: Work well and modern browsers are undefined, so different testers could reach different conclusions.
feedback.incorrect: Work well and modern browsers are undefined, so different testers could reach different conclusions.

content.prompt: All reservation controls must work in the current versions of Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge using keyboard input only.

feedback.correct: The browsers, controls and input method are specified, allowing repeatable compatibility and keyboard tests.
feedback.incorrect: The browsers, controls and input method are specified, allowing repeatable compatibility and keyboard tests.

metadata.title: Problem Decomposition
metadata.summary: Break a complex client problem into manageable technical problems and implementation tasks.
metadata.detail: Work through sub-problems, hierarchy, decomposition quality and requirement mapping.

content.text: Problem Decomposition
This result shows how well you connected client needs to manageable technical problems and implementation tasks.
Identify major problems

Riverside Community Sports Centre needs a digital service where residents create accounts, browse sessions, book or cancel places, and receive confirmation. Staff manage sessions and capacity. The interface must be accessible.

content.prompt: Which four are sensible major sub-problems for the overall service?

feedback.correct: Major sub-problems group related responsibilities. A colour choice is a detail, while build the whole system is too broad to guide implementation.
feedback.incorrect: Major sub-problems group related responsibilities. A colour choice is a detail, while build the whole system is too broad to guide implementation.

content.prompt: Which major problem owns checking whether a session still has a free place?

feedback.correct: Checking and updating available places belongs to capacity management, even though booking uses its result.
feedback.incorrect: Checking and updating available places belongs to capacity management, even though booking uses its result.

content.prompt: Which is a manageable sub-problem for user accounts?

feedback.correct: Validating a defined set of registration fields is specific enough to implement and test.
feedback.incorrect: Validating a defined set of registration fields is specific enough to implement and test.

content.prompt: Which three sub-problems support an accessible booking interface?

options.label: Show errors using text as well as colour

feedback.correct: Labels, keyboard operation and text-based errors create implementable accessibility work. Mandatory drag-and-drop would create a barrier.
feedback.incorrect: Labels, keyboard operation and text-based errors create implementable accessibility work. Mandatory drag-and-drop would create a barrier.

content.prompt: Why should notification delivery be treated as a separate sub-problem from creating a booking record?

options.label: Each has a different responsibility and can fail or be tested independently
They must always use the same function
A booking record never uses data

feedback.correct: Recording the booking and delivering a confirmation are related but distinct responsibilities with different failure cases.
feedback.incorrect: Recording the booking and delivering a confirmation are related but distinct responsibilities with different failure cases.

content.text: Build a problem hierarchy
A useful hierarchy moves from the overall client problem to a major responsibility and then to smaller technical problems.

content.prompt: Order these from broadest problem to smallest technical problem.

feedback.correct: The hierarchy narrows from the overall service, through a major responsibility, to a technical problem and a concrete implementation task.
feedback.incorrect: The hierarchy narrows from the overall service, through a major responsibility, to a technical problem and a concrete implementation task.

content.prompt: Match each smaller technical problem to its major problem.

items.text: Check a submitted password against the stored credential
Filter sessions by activity type and day
Reduce remaining places after a successful booking
Restore a place after a cancellation
Allow staff to create a new session

feedback.correct: Each smaller problem belongs with the major responsibility whose data and behaviour it directly supports.
feedback.incorrect: Each smaller problem belongs with the major responsibility whose data and behaviour it directly supports.

rows.label: Check a submitted password against the stored credential
Filter sessions by activity type and day
Reduce remaining places after a successful booking
Restore a place after a cancellation
Allow staff to create a new session

content.prompt: Which child problem should sit below Send booking confirmation?

options.label: Build a message containing the user, session, date and time
Choose how registration passwords are stored

feedback.correct: Constructing the message data is a smaller problem within the notification responsibility.
feedback.incorrect: Constructing the message data is a smaller problem within the notification responsibility.

content.prompt: What is the best reason to show parent and child problems?

options.label: It shows how detailed implementation work contributes to a larger client need
It hides technical decisions from developers
It guarantees a particular assessment grade

feedback.correct: A hierarchy provides traceability from a broad need to manageable technical work without replacing the requirement itself.
feedback.incorrect: A hierarchy provides traceability from a broad need to manageable technical work without replacing the requirement itself.

content.text: Poor versus effective decomposition
Effective decomposition produces problems that are clear enough to assign, implement and test.

content.prompt: Which decomposition is more useful for implementing a booking?

options.label: Check session exists; check capacity; check eligibility; create booking; update places; return confirmation

feedback.correct: The effective version names distinct problems with observable outcomes. Build booking system is still the original large problem.
feedback.incorrect: The effective version names distinct problems with observable outcomes. Build booking system is still the original large problem.

content.prompt: Which three qualities make a sub-problem useful to a developer?

options.label: It is small enough to implement
It uses broad wording such as sort everything out

feedback.correct: A useful sub-problem has a clear boundary, a checkable outcome and a manageable scope.
feedback.incorrect: A useful sub-problem has a clear boundary, a checkable outcome and a manageable scope.

content.prompt: Why is Create all database code a weak sub-problem?

options.label: It groups unrelated data operations and does not identify the records or behaviours needed

feedback.correct: The phrase hides separate responsibilities such as reading sessions, creating bookings and updating capacity.
feedback.incorrect: The phrase hides separate responsibilities such as reading sessions, creating bookings and updating capacity.

content.prompt: Which revision gives Send notifications a clearer boundary?

options.label: Build confirmation data and request delivery after a successful booking

feedback.correct: The revision identifies the trigger, the required data and the hand-off to delivery.
feedback.incorrect: The revision identifies the trigger, the required data and the hand-off to delivery.

content.text: Map a requirement to implementation problems
Requirement: A resident can book an available session, and the service must prevent the session exceeding its capacity.

content.prompt: Which four technical problems are directly needed for this requirement?

options.label: Identify the resident and selected session

feedback.correct: The four selected problems directly support a valid booking and enforce capacity. Footer colour and payroll are outside this requirement.
feedback.incorrect: The four selected problems directly support a valid booking and enforce capacity. Footer colour and payroll are outside this requirement.

content.prompt: Order the main booking checks and updates into a sensible processing sequence.

feedback.correct: The service must find and validate the session before writing changes, then return confirmation after the booking succeeds.
feedback.incorrect: The service must find and validate the session before writing changes, then return confirmation after the booking succeeds.

content.prompt: Match each technical problem to a possible implementation task.

categories.label: Insert resident_id and session_id into Bookings
Check for an existing resident/session pair
Build a response with booking ID and session details

feedback.correct: Each implementation task is a concrete way to solve its technical problem while keeping traceability to the requirement.
feedback.incorrect: Each implementation task is a concrete way to solve its technical problem while keeping traceability to the requirement.

options.label: Insert resident_id and session_id into Bookings
Check for an existing resident/session pair
Build a response with booking ID and session details

content.prompt: How does this mapping help later testing?

options.label: Each technical problem suggests focused checks and expected outcomes

feedback.correct: The mapped problems reveal testable decisions such as no capacity, duplicate booking and successful confirmation.
feedback.incorrect: The mapped problems reveal testable decisions such as no capacity, duplicate booking and successful confirmation.

metadata.title: Data Design Knowledge Check
metadata.summary: Check the building blocks used to describe data, relationships and validation rules.
metadata.detail: Use a college clubs dataset to reason about types, keys, relationships and a data dictionary.

content.text: Data Design Knowledge Check
Use this summary to identify which data-design building blocks need more practice before designing a larger solution.
Fields, records and tables
Northbridge College stores information about students, clubs and club memberships. Begin with the structure of a relational dataset.

content.prompt: Match each data term to the example.

items.text: All student records with the same columns
The real-world Student concept being described

feedback.correct: A field stores one attribute, a record combines fields for one instance, a table holds consistent records and an entity is the concept represented.
feedback.incorrect: A field stores one attribute, a record combines fields for one instance, a table holds consistent records and an entity is the concept represented.

rows.label: All student records with the same columns
The real-world Student concept being described

content.prompt: Which description is a record?

options.label: One row containing all stored values for club C12
The rule that capacity must be positive

feedback.correct: A record is one complete row about one instance, such as one club.
feedback.incorrect: A record is one complete row about one instance, such as one club.

content.prompt: Why should every record in a table use the same defined fields?

options.label: It keeps the structure consistent for storage, validation and processing
It guarantees every value is unique
It makes all text the same length

feedback.correct: A consistent schema lets the solution interpret, validate and query each record reliably.
feedback.incorrect: A consistent schema lets the solution interpret, validate and query each record reliably.

content.prompt: Which name follows a clear, consistent field naming convention?

feedback.correct: joined_on is concise, meaningful and follows a predictable lowercase underscore convention. Other conventions can also work when applied consistently.
feedback.incorrect: joined_on is concise, meaningful and follows a predictable lowercase underscore convention. Other conventions can also work when applied consistently.

content.text: Data types and field design
Choose conceptual data types that suit the meaning and operations required by each field.

content.prompt: Which conceptual type best fits student_id values such as S00107?

feedback.correct: The ID contains a letter and leading zeroes, and it is an identifier rather than a value used in arithmetic.
feedback.incorrect: The ID contains a letter and leading zeroes, and it is an identifier rather than a value used in arithmetic.

content.prompt: Which conceptual type best fits a club capacity of 24 places?

feedback.correct: Capacity is a count of whole places, so an integer supports comparison and arithmetic.
feedback.incorrect: Capacity is a count of whole places, so an integer supports comparison and arithmetic.

content.prompt: Which conceptual type best fits a weekly fee of 7.50?

feedback.correct: A decimal type represents values with a fractional part. Financial systems may use a dedicated fixed-precision money representation.
feedback.incorrect: A decimal type represents values with a fractional part. Financial systems may use a dedicated fixed-precision money representation.

content.prompt: Which conceptual type best fits whether a membership is active?

feedback.correct: A two-state active flag maps naturally to true or false.
feedback.incorrect: A two-state active flag maps naturally to true or false.

content.prompt: Why set a sensible maximum length for club_name?

options.label: It documents the expected data and prevents unexpectedly large values
It makes every club name unique
It converts the name into a number

feedback.correct: A justified length supports validation, storage planning and interface design, but it does not create uniqueness or required status.
feedback.incorrect: A justified length supports validation, storage planning and interface design, but it does not create uniqueness or required status.

content.text: Keys and relationships
Use the accessible entity representation to identify keys and the relationships created by a membership record.

content.prompt: Which field is the primary key of Student?

feedback.correct: student_id is intended to identify each student record uniquely and remain stable when a name changes.
feedback.incorrect: student_id is intended to identify each student record uniquely and remain stable when a name changes.

content.prompt: Which two fields are foreign keys in Membership?

feedback.correct: student_id links to Student and club_id links to Club. They are foreign keys because they refer to primary keys in other tables.
feedback.incorrect: student_id links to Student and club_id links to Club. They are foreign keys because they refer to primary keys in other tables.

content.prompt: What relationship exists from Club to Membership?

options.label: Many clubs must share one membership record

feedback.correct: One club can have many membership records, while each membership record refers to one club.
feedback.incorrect: One club can have many membership records, while each membership record refers to one club.

Use this summary to review when each testing method is useful and what a test record should communicate.
Classify testing scenarios
Choose the most appropriate method for each scenario. Testing labels can overlap: a unit test may be automated, while black-box describes testing behaviour without relying on internal code knowledge.

feedback.incorrect: Integration testing checks whether two or more components exchange data and work together correctly.

feedback.incorrect: System testing evaluates the complete integrated solution against its requirements.

feedback.incorrect: User acceptance testing asks whether the solution is acceptable for the client's real needs and agreed criteria.

A useful test case records enough information for another person to repeat the check and understand the outcome.

feedback.correct: The selected fields provide traceability, repeatable data, a comparison between expected and actual outcomes, and a recorded status. Real credentials must not be used.

content.text: Testing and iteration
Testing becomes valuable development evidence when its findings lead to a change and the change is checked again.

content.prompt: Order the testing and improvement cycle.

options.label: To verify the change fixes the defect and has not broken related behaviour
To erase the original test record

feedback.incorrect: Retesting provides evidence that the intended fix works. Relevant regression checks look for unintended effects elsewhere.

options.label: Record the actual result, inspect the range condition, correct it and rerun boundary tests

metadata.title: Define Oakridge business requirements, scope and value
metadata.summary: Write first-pass business requirements, an in-scope / out-of-scope boundary, and value statements grounded in Weeks 1–2.
metadata.detail: Write first-pass business requirements, an in-scope / out-of-scope boundary, and value statements grounded in Weeks 1–2.

content.text: From research notes to a project proposal

Specification 1.1 moves from familiarisation into planning and requirement analysis. You explore the brief and define the scope of an intended solution as a project proposal. This week you start that proposal. You do not yet write full functional and non-functional requirements, KPIs or acceptance criteria — that is the next teaching week.
Business requirements

Business requirements describe what the organisation needs the work to achieve: new software, an amendment to current practice, or better security and evidence. For Oakridge, examples include a single place to see workshops, digital registers that tutors will actually use, and reports the manager can give funders. They are not yet 'the system shall...' product requirements.
Scope is a professional no

Scope says what this project will and will not attempt. Out of scope might include payroll, a full college finance suite, or biometric registers you could not justify in Week 2. A clear no protects the Occupational Specialism later: you can show you understood the brief without promising the world.
Value to users and to the organisation

Value must be stated for learners and tutors as well as for the centre. Learner value might be fewer missed sessions. Organisational value might be fewer hours assembling funder evidence, or fewer room clashes. If you cannot say how you would notice the value, it is still a slogan.

content.title: Assessment habit
content.text: Task 1 of the Occupational Specialism expects analysis that later design can be traced back to. Requirements that ignore your own research log will not survive that trace.
Practical application

content.prompt: Write three Oakridge business requirements. Each must be traceable to the brief or to your Week 2 evidence log.
content.guidance: Look for single timetable, digital registers, funder evidence, phone-and-PC access, or low-training tutor use. Cite the brief or research.

content.prompt: State what is in scope for a first release and two things that are out of scope, with a one-line justification for each exclusion.
content.placeholder: In scope: ... Out of scope: ... because...
content.guidance: Exclusions should cite budget, staffing, un-evidenced needs, or high-risk ideas parked in Week 2 such as biometrics or a full MIS.

content.prompt: Write one value statement for a user group and one for the organisation. Include how you would notice if the value appeared.
content.placeholder: User value: ... We would notice by... Organisation: ...
content.guidance: User value might be fewer missed sessions, noticed through attendance. Organisation value might be hours saved on reports.

content.text: Previous: Week 2 evidence log. Do not let students write full NFRs today. Formative classification follows. Next lessons decompose and abstract this scope so Week 4 can add functional/NFR/KPI/acceptance detail.

content.prompt: What is decomposition for in specification 1.1?

Treat the product name as a requirement

metadata.title: Decompose Oakridge and recognise patterns
metadata.summary: Break the scoped problem into parts and compare those parts with patterns from existing adult-learning or booking systems.
metadata.detail: Break the scoped problem into parts and compare those parts with patterns from existing adult-learning or booking systems.

content.text: Split the problem, then look for patterns

Specification 1.1 asks you to apply decomposition, pattern recognition and abstraction to split the problem into discrete objects. Lesson 2 covers the first two. Lesson 3 covers abstraction. This is the same computational thinking you practised in Foundations, now applied to a live client after two weeks of research.
Decomposition that a third party can follow

Name parts as problems or processes, not as screens. Useful Oakridge parts might include: publishing the workshop offer; learner booking; tutor register; room allocation; funder reporting; user accounts. If a part is still the whole system, split again. If a part is 'make it look nice', it is not yet a problem part.
Pattern recognition

Look across your Week 1–2 research. Booking flows, attendance registers and report exports appear in many products. That pattern is useful. A parent portal or payroll module in a college suite is a pattern that probably does not apply. Pattern recognition also includes risks: many centres fail when sessional tutors will not change their register habit.
Practical application

content.prompt: Decompose the in-scope Oakridge problem into 5–7 named parts. One sentence each on what that part is for.
content.guidance: Expect booking, registers, reporting, accounts, rooming, notifications. Reject payroll, HR or biometrics if they were out of scope.

content.prompt: Choose two parts. For each, name a pattern from an existing solution and say whether Oakridge should reuse, adapt or reject it.
content.guidance: A strong answer cites a researched product or common workflow and Oakridge constraints such as phones, tutor training or funder reports.

content.text: Foundations problem-decomposition remains available as extra practice; this lesson must stay on Oakridge. Formative follows. Next lesson abstracts these parts into a proposal that hides premature detail.

content.text: Starter retrieval

content.prompt: What does abstraction ask you to do in specification 1.1?

options.label: Keep the details that matter for this stage and hide those that do not

feedback.correct: Abstraction filters. You still need inputs, outputs, what varies and what stays constant — not the full stack.

Whether learners book on phones belongs now; exact CSS colours can wait

options.label: It stops the proposal drowning in detail so requirements can be written against a clear model

feedback.incorrect: Abstraction prepares requirements work. It does not replace it.

metadata.title: Abstract the Oakridge proposal
metadata.summary: Decide what must remain visible in the project proposal and what can be hidden until design, data modelling or implementation.
metadata.detail: Decide what must remain visible in the project proposal and what can be hidden until design, data modelling or implementation.

content.text: Hide the right details

Specification 1.1 abstraction includes knowing what information is needed, filtering out noise, and hiding internal workings. You should be able to say what inputs are needed, what outputs and outcomes are expected, what will vary, what stays constant, the key actions the solution must perform, and which processes repeat.
A proposal-level model

For Oakridge, constants might include the existing classroom PCs, the need for funder reports, and the lack of an IT team. Variations might include workshop topics, tutor availability and whether a session is in a classroom or the hall. Repeated processes include booking, taking a register and issuing a reminder. Internal workings — tables, APIs, class names — can stay hidden this week.

content.title: Progression
content.text: Week 4 will add functional and non-functional requirements, KPIs, constraints and acceptance criteria onto this abstract model. If the model is still a product name, Week 4 will collapse into solutioneering.
Practical application

content.prompt: For the register part, list the inputs needed, the expected outputs or outcomes, one thing that varies and one thing that stays constant.
content.guidance: Inputs might include learner list and present/absent. Outputs include an attendance record. Variation: hall vs classroom. Constant: evidence for funders.

content.prompt: Name two details you will hide from the Week 3 proposal and say when they should reappear.
content.guidance: Examples: CSS, exact schema, language choice, vendor. They reappear at design, data design or implementation.

content.prompt: List the key actions the in-scope solution must perform, using the parts from Lesson 2. Mark any that repeat.
content.placeholder: Publish offer (repeat each term); book place; ...
content.guidance: Expect publish, book, register, report, notify. Repeats should be explicit.

content.text: Formative follows. Homework is the proposal outline. Check that students can point to Weeks 1–2 evidence inside the proposal. If abstraction has become vagueness, send them back to named parts.

metadata.title: Baseline diagnostic: technologies you already use
metadata.summary: Identify digital technologies you already use and examples you believe are new or emerging.
metadata.detail: Identify digital technologies you already use and examples you believe are new or emerging.

content.text: Baseline diagnostic
This unit is Exploring New and Emerging Digital Technologies. Before new definitions, record what you already know. There are no marks for a 'right' baseline — it shows your starting point.

content.prompt: List five digital technologies you use in a normal week. Include devices, apps or services.
content.placeholder: For example: smartphone, contactless payment, cloud storage...

content.prompt: Name two technologies you believe are new or emerging, and say why you think they are emerging rather than established.
A supermarket has used barcode scanners at checkouts for decades. How should you classify barcode scanning today?

options.label: Emerging, because shops still update the software
Established current technology that is widely adopted

feedback.correct: Widespread, long-standing use makes this established current technology. Updates do not by themselves make it emerging.
feedback.incorrect: Established tools can still be digital. Emerging means the technology is still developing or not yet widely adopted.

metadata.title: Define established, current and emerging technology
metadata.summary: Use contemporary examples to distinguish established, current and emerging digital technologies.
metadata.detail: Use contemporary examples to distinguish established, current and emerging digital technologies.

content.text: Current and emerging digital technology

LO1 asks you to know about new and emerging digital technologies. AC 1.1 later asks you to outline them. Start with clear definitions so later weeks on mobile, IoT, cloud and AI have a shared language.
Useful definitions

Established technology is widely adopted and no longer changing the way a sector works by itself. Current technology is in common use now. Emerging technology is still developing, not yet adopted by most users or organisations, or is starting to change how people live or work. The same technology can be emerging in one sector and current in another.

content.title: Contemporary examples
content.text: Established: desktop PCs in offices, barcode checkout. Current: smartphones, contactless payments, cloud storage. Emerging (varies by sector): generative AI assistants, consumer 5G features, warehouse robotics, clinical VR training.
Why adoption differs

Individuals may adopt a smart watch for fitness while a hospital waits for clinical evidence. A bank may trial AI fraud detection while a small retailer still uses a till. Cost, skills, regulation, customer trust and existing systems all affect adoption.

content.prompt: In your own words, define current digital technology and emerging digital technology. Give one example of each.
content.placeholder: Current means... Example: ... Emerging means... Example: ...
content.guidance: Current = in common use now. Emerging = still developing or not yet widely adopted. Examples should match the definition.

content.prompt: Choose one technology that might be current in one industry and emerging in another. Explain the difference.
content.placeholder: For example drones in film versus drones in NHS logistics...
content.guidance: A strong answer names two sectors and an adoption reason such as regulation, cost or skills.

content.text: SoL Week 1: baseline diagnostic then tutor demonstration of established/current/emerging. UDL: visual examples, short definitions, discussion. Scaffold: start with familiar devices. Challenge: differences in adoption between industries. Industry examples: retail, banking, entertainment, healthcare, manufacturing, IT.

content.text: Classify the examples

A warehouse using autonomous picking robots

Using a landline as the only way to contact a business
A GP surgery trialling VR for surgical training
Storing schoolwork in cloud storage
A high-street shop still using only a cash till and paper receipts

feedback.incorrect: Ask whether most people or organisations already use it. Widespread use is current; limited or experimental use is emerging.

content.text: Starter retrieval

content.prompt: Which statement best describes an emerging digital technology?

A technology that cannot be used by businesses

feedback.incorrect: Focus on how new and how widely adopted the technology is.

options.label: Safety, evidence and regulation often slow adoption in healthcare

feedback.correct: Sector context changes adoption. Healthcare has higher safety and regulatory barriers than entertainment.

options.label: When a new capability, such as on-device AI, is not yet widely used

feedback.incorrect: Separate the device from new features that are not yet widely adopted.

metadata.summary: Classify a range of technologies and discuss why adoption may differ between individuals, organisations and sectors.
metadata.detail: Classify a range of technologies and discuss why adoption may differ between individuals, organisations and sectors.

content.text: The same technology, different adoption

Work with structured technology cards across retail, banking, entertainment, healthcare, manufacturing and IT. For each example, decide whether it is mainly personal, organisational, or both, and whether it is current or emerging in that sector.
Industry snapshots

Retail: self-checkout, mobile shopping apps, warehouse robots. Banking: contactless cards, mobile banking, AI fraud alerts. Entertainment: streaming, recommendation systems, VR. Healthcare: electronic records, remote appointments, surgical robots. Manufacturing: sensors on production lines, cobots. IT: cloud hosting, automated testing, generative AI coding assistants.

content.prompt: Choose one retail technology. Is it mainly current or emerging, and who adopts it first — shoppers or the retailer?
content.placeholder: Technology: ... Current/emerging because... First adopted by...
content.guidance: Mobile apps are current for many shoppers. Warehouse robotics is still emerging for many retailers.

content.prompt: Explain why a healthcare example might be adopted more slowly than a similar entertainment example.
content.guidance: Look for safety, data protection, clinical evidence and staff training, not 'hospitals are old-fashioned'.

content.prompt: Give one example of a technology an individual might use every day that a small organisation has not adopted yet. Explain the gap.
content.placeholder: Individuals use... Small organisations may not because...
content.guidance: Cost, skills, trust or 'good enough' existing processes are typical reasons.

content.text: SoL guided learning: classify technologies and discuss adoption differences. UDL: technology cards. Challenge: compare industries. Cultural capital: how technological change affects everyday life, employment and access to services.

Streaming music on a phone

A clinic piloting AI to draft patient letters for clinician review

feedback.correct: Phones and streaming are personal and current. Bank apps and EPOS are organisational and current. Lights-out factories and clinical AI remain emerging in many organisations.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who the main user is, then how widely that group has already adopted it.

A list of every technology in the unit

content.text: One technology, one clear outline

Choose one emerging technology. Produce a short profile: name; whether it is emerging and why; who uses it; one personal or business use; and one industry where it matters. You will reuse this habit in later weeks and in Assignment 1 (AC 1.1).

content.title: Sensible choices this early
content.text: Pick something you can explain: consumer IoT, mobile payments, cloud storage, wearables, a simple AI assistant, or contactless NFC. Avoid a topic you can only name from a headline.

content.prompt: Write the profile: technology name; why it is emerging; who uses it; one use; one industry example.
content.placeholder: Name: ... Emerging because: ... Users: ... Use: ... Industry: ...
content.guidance: Check the 'why emerging' sentence is about adoption or development, not 'because it is cool'.

content.prompt: Name the source you used (site, video, article) and one reason it is good enough for class research.
content.guidance: A named organisation, manufacturer, or reputable news/education source is stronger than an anonymous post.

content.text: Exit check

content.prompt: Current digital technology is best described as technology that is...

options.label: Always the same as emerging technology

feedback.correct: Current means widely used now. Emerging is still developing or not yet widely adopted.
feedback.incorrect: Current = common use now.

content.prompt: Which is the best emerging example for many organisations in 2026?

options.label: A fully autonomous store with no staff, still being trialled

feedback.correct: Trials of staff-free stores are not yet normal. Email and mice are established.
feedback.incorrect: Pick the example that is not yet widely adopted.

content.prompt: Why include different industries when outlining emerging technologies?

options.label: Because every technology is used in the same way everywhere
Because the same technology can be used differently in retail, healthcare, banking or manufacturing

feedback.correct: LO1 includes how technologies are used in different industries. Context changes the application.
feedback.incorrect: Industry examples show different uses, not just a longer list of brand names.

content.prompt: Outline one emerging technology and one way it is used in a named industry.

content.text: Independent study
Find three technologies you meet in everyday life that you consider emerging. For each, outline what it is and how it is used. Bring the list to Week 2 (Mobile Technology).

content.prompt: Technology 1: name, why it is emerging, and its everyday use.
Technology 2: name, why it is emerging, and its everyday use.
Technology 3: name, why it is emerging, and its everyday use.
Which of your three examples, if any, depends on a smartphone? Week 2 looks at mobile technology in more depth.

metadata.detail: Retrieve the distinction between current and emerging technologies and identify developments in mobile devices.

content.text: Starter retrieval
Week 1 defined current and emerging technology. Week 2 looks at mobile technology: smartphones, tablets and other devices that people carry.

content.prompt: A smartphone is current for most people. Which feature might still be emerging?

options.label: On-device AI that summarises photos without a clear user understanding of where data goes

feedback.correct: The device can be current while a new capability is still emerging.
feedback.incorrect: Separate the established phone from newer capabilities that are not yet widely understood or adopted.

content.prompt: Which list best describes what makes a device 'mobile technology'?

options.label: It must run desktop Windows only
It combines portable computing, communication, sensors, apps and internet connectivity
It cannot connect to the internet
It is only used in factories

feedback.correct: Mobile technology is portable and typically combines those elements.
feedback.incorrect: Think portable computing plus communication, sensors, apps and connectivity.

content.prompt: Name two developments in mobile devices from the last few years (hardware, sensors, apps or connectivity).

metadata.title: How mobile technologies combine several capabilities
metadata.summary: See how mobile devices combine computing, communication, sensors, applications and internet connectivity.
metadata.detail: See how mobile devices combine computing, communication, sensors, applications and internet connectivity.

content.text: More than a phone
Outline mobile technology by its parts, not just by brand. A typical smartphone is a computer, a communicator, a sensor pack, an app platform and an internet client.
Five parts to look for

Computing: processor, storage, operating system. Communication: calls, messages, email. Sensors: GPS, camera, accelerometer, fingerprint or face unlock. Applications: banking, maps, health, work apps. Connectivity: Wi-Fi, mobile data, Bluetooth, NFC.

content.title: Not only phones
content.text: Tablets, handheld payment devices, delivery scanners and some wearables are also mobile technology. Week 6 looks at wearables in more depth; today stay on phones, tablets and similar handheld devices.

content.prompt: Outline mobile technology in four to six sentences using the five parts above.
content.placeholder: Mobile technology is... It includes... Sensors... Apps... Connectivity...
content.guidance: A good outline names portable computing, communication, sensors, apps and connectivity without copying a vendor advert.

content.prompt: Choose one sensor on a smartphone and explain one personal use and one possible business use.
content.guidance: GPS for maps versus delivery tracking; camera for photos versus scanning parcels; NFC for tap-to-pay versus staff badges.

content.text: SoL teacher demonstration: mobile technologies combine computing, communication, sensors, applications and internet connectivity. UDL: familiar devices and screenshots. Next lesson splits personal and organisational applications.

metadata.title: Progress check: characteristics of mobile technology
metadata.summary: Identify key characteristics of mobile technology.
metadata.detail: Identify key characteristics of mobile technology.

content.text: Is it a mobile-technology characteristic?

content.prompt: Classify each statement.

items.label: The device is designed to be carried and used in different locations
It can run applications
It must be a desktop tower under a desk
It can connect to networks such as Wi-Fi or mobile data
It often includes sensors such as GPS or a camera
It can only be used by software developers

feedback.correct: Portability, apps, connectivity and sensors are core. Desktop towers and 'developers only' are not.
feedback.incorrect: Ask whether the statement is true of phones and tablets that people carry.

metadata.detail: Retrieve key characteristics of mobile technology before comparing personal and business applications.

content.text: Starter retrieval

content.prompt: NFC on a phone is mainly an example of which mobile capability?

options.label: Short-range communication, for example contactless payments

feedback.correct: NFC is short-range communication used in payments and similar taps.
feedback.incorrect: NFC is about tapping the phone near a reader, not about desktop hardware.

content.prompt: Why do organisations care that staff have mobile devices?

options.label: Because phones cannot access the internet
Because work can continue away from a desk: communication, data capture and customer service
Because mobile devices cannot run apps
Because sensors never collect useful data

feedback.correct: Business value is access and action away from a fixed PC.
feedback.incorrect: Think field work, customer apps and staff communication.

metadata.title: Personal and business applications of mobile devices
metadata.summary: Compare personal and organisational applications of smartphones, tablets and other mobile devices.
metadata.detail: Compare personal and organisational applications of smartphones, tablets and other mobile devices.

content.text: Same device, different jobs

Personal uses include messaging, maps, photos, entertainment, health tracking and mobile payments. Organisational uses include mobile banking, retail apps, field working, delivery scanning and healthcare records at the bedside. The hardware overlaps; the purpose changes.
Compare requirements

A learner using maps needs battery and GPS. A delivery driver also needs a rugged device, a work account, barcode scanning and a data connection that works on the road. Extension: different users need different security, durability and apps.

content.prompt: Describe two personal applications of a mobile device and the capability each one uses (app, sensor, connectivity or communication).
Describe two business applications, using different sectors if you can (for example banking, retail, delivery or healthcare).
Pick one personal use and one business use of the same capability (for example GPS or the camera). What extra requirement does the business use have?
content.guidance: Look for security, audit trails, shared accounts, durability or working hours.

content.text: SoL guided learning: compare personal and organisational applications. Industry: mobile banking, retail, field working, delivery, healthcare. Scaffold: structured prompts. Challenge: compare requirements for different users.

content.prompt: Is the main purpose personal or organisational?

items.label: A customer checking a bank balance in an app
A learner sending a message to a friend
A courier scanning a parcel with a handheld device
Someone using a phone camera for holiday photos
A nurse recording observations on a ward tablet

content.prompt: Which is the clearest organisational benefit of mobile access?

options.label: Staff can only work at one desk
Customers or staff can complete a task away from a branch or office
The organisation must stop using any security
Mobile devices cannot connect to data

metadata.title: Produce a short organisational mobile case study
metadata.summary: Show how mobile technology supports a selected organisation.
metadata.detail: Show how mobile technology supports a selected organisation.

content.text: Case study, not a product advert

Choose an organisation you know or can research: a bank, supermarket, delivery firm, GP practice, college or local shop. Explain how mobile technology supports that organisation. Include who uses the device, what they do, and one benefit.

content.title: Use this structure
content.text: Organisation and sector. Mobile technology used. Who uses it (customers, employees or both). What task it supports. One benefit. One possible limitation (battery, coverage, security or training).

content.prompt: Write the case study using the structure above (about 150–220 words).
content.guidance: Check it is a real or realistic organisation, names a mobile use, and includes a benefit plus a limitation.

content.text: SoL independent application. Homework extends this to customer or employee communication specifically. Review key terminology at the end of the lesson.

content.text: Terminology check

content.prompt: GPS on a phone is best described as...

options.label: A location sensor used by maps and many business tracking apps

feedback.correct: GPS is a location sensor with personal and business applications.
feedback.incorrect: GPS is about location, not printing or desktop OS.

content.prompt: A tablet used on a hospital ward is mainly an example of...

options.label: A personal gaming hobby with no organisational purpose
An organisational mobile device supporting staff work

feedback.incorrect: The user is staff doing work, so it is a business application.

content.text: Independent study

Pick one organisation. Find out how it uses mobile technology to communicate with customers or employees: app notifications, SMS, staff handhelds, or a customer app. Bring this to Week 3, which starts consumer Internet of Things.

content.prompt: Organisation, sector, and who is being communicated with (customers, employees or both).
How mobile technology is used for that communication, and one benefit.
Does this organisation also use connected objects (not just phones), such as scanners, trackers or smart speakers? Week 3 introduces consumer IoT.
